title: Why Students Don’t Get Literature
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Answering a reader's question about weak Year 10 students who meander around plot, Dominic Salles argues that we have taught them that a text's importance is its plot rather than the author's ideas. He proposes teaching from day one the recurring big ideas of literature, such as the human condition, morality and religion, politics, class and the role of women, so students build schema across texts. His fixes are cross-text comparison questions, teaching through model essays at grades 5, 7 and 9 in booklets, DARTS-style cloze and reconstruction tasks, and polarising essay prompts. He claims these give students a conversation with the text rather than with the teacher about the exam.
points: Students meander around plot because they have been taught that plot, character and setting matter in themselves, not as vehicles for the author's ideas.
Teaching a small set of recurring big ideas lets students link texts, track change across literary movements and build schema that serves revision.
Forcing cross-text comparisons engages students with authors' ideas and strengthens knowledge of both texts.
Model essays at grades 5, 7 and 9, worked through with DARTS cloze and reconstruction tasks, can give weaker students an early 80% success rate with above-level writing.
Polarising prompts such as 'Is Lord of the Flies a Christian or an atheist text?' convey that the real conversation is about ideas.
quotes: The reason for this is actually quite simple: we have taught them that the importance of a text is the plot.
Instead, students treat texts like movies - something to sit through, slightly less interesting than watching it on a big screen.
We fail to teach them that a text is a conversation between the author and the reader about the society they both live in and the future they could build.
Rather than having a conversation with the text, they only have a conversation with the teacher about what they need to pass, viewing the text as a mere hurdle between them and an exam grade.
Getting students to make these comparisons forces them to engage in a meaningful way with the author’s ideas, which will strengthen their knowledge of both texts.

While this sounds tedious and boring, in the classroom it is fast-paced, challenging, and rewarding because students quickly build an 80% success rate, even when dealing with essays that are 1, 2, or 3 grades above their current performance.
None of these are the kinds of questions GCSE exams ask, but they are much more interesting.
